book: 001 - Seinfeld and Philosophy - A Book about Everything and Nothing

chapters.file: ch03 - Popular Culture and Philosophy Series Editor George A. Reisch.md

chapters.relation: Editor William Irwin's introduction explains why Seinfeld is philosophical: 'Seinfeld' sounds like German for 'field of being,' echoing Heidegger's Sein und Zeit, and he tells students to picture the four at Monk's coffee shop when Heidegger describes the 'idle chatter' of the inauthentic mode of being, while George's 'what is the opposite of what I would normally do?' shows the courage of changing one's way of seeing. He frames the whole book with Socrates' claim that the unexamined life is not worth living - the Seinfeld characters examine their lives constantly, though Socrates would approve of neither their lives nor their examinations - and with Nietzsche's 'A Book for None and All' subtitle, then lays out the volume's four-act structure.

chapters.file: ch08 - Act I - The Characters, aka “The New York Four”.md
ch09 - The Fates of Socrates and Seinfeld.md
chapters.relation: William Irwin compares Jerry and Socrates: the 'Jerry problem' of whether the fictional Jerry is the real Jerry (complicated by Seinlanguage) mirrors the Socratic problem of separating Socrates from Plato's dialogues. Jerry, like Socrates the gadfly, provokes his circle with questions that hunt for essences - the black-and-white cookie, 'is soup a meal?' - and shares Socrates' irony (the 'War: What Is It Good For?' gag in 'The Marine Biologist' works exactly like Socratic shamming ignorance). But where Socrates died serenely per the Apology and Phaedo, Jerry is self-absorbed and ends the series convicted under the Good Samaritan law, doing his stand-up 'gadfly' routine for prison inmates - an examined life, but not an exemplary one.

chapters.file: ch10 - George and Virtue—Like Oil and Water.md
chapters.relation: Daniel Barwick runs George through Aristotle's function argument and finds him wanting: a paradigm of 'the many' who thinks happiness is fortune and momentary victories over others (free parking, perfect airport pickups) rather than activity of the soul in accordance with virtue. His 'do the opposite' epiphany in 'The Opposite' embraces the more extreme vice rather than steering toward the rationally chosen mean, and his self-hatred, laziness, and pleasure-seeking fail all three of Aristotle's tips for hitting the mean. Since George will never practice virtuous action until it becomes habit, Barwick concludes George is doomed to his miserable existence - which is, conveniently for us, why he is funny.

Sarah Worth asks whether Elaine is a feminist icon or 'just one of the boys.' Elaine passes every liberal-feminist benchmark - a Tufts education, the only steady career (Pendant Publishing, then the J. Peterman catalogue), financial and emotional independence - but fails the ethic of care: her dating ethics run on pettiness (dumping men for not offering pie, for dirty bathrooms, over Puddy's high-fiving), the 'spongeworthy' episode commodifies her own relationships, she shows no maternal instinct toward the ugly baby, and she secretly resents George's engagement. The conclusion: being one of the boys does not a feminist make, though Elaine still models an independence the women of Friends and Frasier lack.

William Irwin argues Kramer is Kierkegaard's aesthete par excellence: his endless abandoned schemes (make-your-own-pizza, beach-smelling cologne, Kramerica Industries), his aliases (H.E. Pennypacker, Dr. Van Nostrand), and his 'Kavorka' revolving door of women enact Either/Or's 'crop rotation' method and the Diary of the Seducer, all flight from the despair hinted at in 'The Switch' ('All this time I'm trying not to be me'). His brief office job in 'The Bizarro Jerry' - 'structure... TCB, taking care of business' - is a flirtation with Judge William's ethical stage of commitment, and Irwin closes with a thought experiment: could Kramer ever make the leap of faith to the religious stage, performing his own teleological suspension of the ethical like Abraham?

chapters.file: ch13 - Act II - Seinfeld and the Philosophers.md
ch14 - Was it a Show about Nothing.md
chapters.relation: Eric Bronson takes George's NBC pitch for 'a show about nothing' as a live philosophical problem: Parmenides argued we cannot meaningfully speak of what-is-not (so Art Vandelay is unsayable), but Plato's Sophist answers that nothing is 'otherness' with real power - the puffy shirt is something other than beautiful, and 'The Parking Garage' is doing something other than what is interesting or useful. Lao Tzu's Tao Te Ching goes further: the nameless Tao begets the ten thousand things, and wei wu wei (action through non-action) conquers, as in 'The Chinese Restaurant', where a whole episode of standing in line doing nothing is itself something happening.

chapters.file: ch15 - The Seinfeldians as Fixed Essences.md
chapters.relation: Mark Conard notes the show's relentless recurrences - Kramer sliding through the door, 'Newman!', George's firings, the Puddy on-again-off-again loop - and asks whether this is Nietzsche's eternal recurrence. It cannot be, since Nietzsche's cosmos is a flux of recombining centers of force; things recur in Seinfeld precisely because nothing changes. The Seinfeldians are instead fixed Platonic Forms or essences: 'The Bizarro Jerry' proves it, since only an unchanging archetype can have an exact opposite (Kevin, Gene, Feldman, Vargas), and the backwards episode 'The Betrayal' works only because characters exempt from time and change cannot develop.

chapters.file: ch16 - No Exit and The Vault Sartre and Seinfeld on the Inescapability of Others.md
chapters.relation: Jennifer McMahon defends the heretical reading of Sartre as a relational theorist of the self: in Being and Nothingness consciousness is a nothingness, not an essential ego, and only the Other - 'the Other accomplishes... to see ourselves as we are' - lets us grasp ourselves as objects. Seinfeld illustrates this better than Sartre's own suspicion of others: Jerry's identity exists only through his entanglement with George, Kramer, and Elaine (change them and you get a 'bizarro-Jerry'), and the finale's prison cell ('The Vault') replays No Exit's locked room with the trial's parade of wounded minor characters - except that Seinfeld's chattering foursome shows friendship as a positive, not hellish, dependency.

Kelly Dean Jolley reads Seinfeld as the sitcom twin of Wittgenstein's Philosophical Investigations: both are 'albums' - remarks, vignettes - that refuse the normal form (the finished essay, the developed plot), and both try to make us notice the commonplace hidden by its very familiarity (PI sections 118, 129, 596 on feelings of familiarity and the attack on meaning as a mental act). Jerry's 'It's a show about nothing' is the show's version of Wittgenstein's destroying houses of cards: the plot was the illusion, and the vignettes nag, repeat, and transpose the commonplaces until we hear what he calls the 'tune of our lives.'

chapters.file: ch18 - Act III - Untimely Meditations by the Water Cooler.md

chapters.relation: Jason Holt asks whether it is rational for George to 'do the opposite' and answers no. Distinguishing minimal, medial, and maximal rationality, he argues the Costanza Maneuver is neither reliable (its .800 batting average in 'The Opposite' is dumb luck - insulting Steinbrenner into a job and cowing movie thugs should not work) nor feasible: George's akrasia and impulse problems betray him, and the opposite of an action is usually indeterminate (Jerry: 'chicken salad is not the opposite of tuna... salmon swim against the current'). Since George knows all this, betting on the Maneuver is irrational - its success is precisely the joke, 'not as good, works better.'

chapters.file: ch20 - Mr. Peterman, the Wicked Witch of the West, and Me.md
chapters.relation: Norah Martin uses J. Peterman to explain ideology through irony rather than cynicism: we know the catalogue's 'pointless drivel' is fiction, yet we buy anyway - Žižek's 'fetishists in practice, not in theory' - so that laughing at the absurd narratives is the catalogue's best advertising. Peterman himself, who must buy Kramer's life stories because his own life is only what Elaine writes, is the most realistic character: like the Wicked Witch of the West (not the Wizard with a humbug behind the curtain), there is literally nothing beneath the costume, showing that the unified Cartesian subject is a 'primordial lie' and that Jerry's superficiality ('I'm being as superficial as I possibly can') is the honest response.

chapters.file: ch21 - What’s so Funny about That.md
chapters.relation: Jorge Gracia proposes that we laugh at the significance of the insignificant and cry at the insignificance of the significant, then reads 'The Outing' nearly scene by scene: the eavesdropped 'just because you two are homosexuals' joke, the washed pear, the whiny voice on tape, Kramer's 'I thought we were going to take a steam,' and the refrain 'not that there's anything wrong with that.' The episode is funny because it lays bare society's stereotype of the gay man (thin, single, neat) and its duplicity - everyone disavows bigotry in exactly the breath with which they panic at being thought gay - turning an insignificant coffee-shop prank into a mirror of well-intentioned bigotry.

chapters.file: ch22 - Act IV - Is There Anything Wrong with That.md

chapters.relation: Robert Epperson defends the show against the 'no hugging, no learning' charge by arguing Seinfeld is about the pursuit of the moral life: the four constantly consult each other on right conduct (gift-giving, break-up timing, obligations to friends and parents), distinguishing the moral life from mere integrity. He grades each character - Kramer is Plato's man of right opinion without knowledge whose one maxim is 'listen to your little man,' George means rightly but is the man of wrong opinion, Elaine is undone by indecisiveness, Jerry is the moral axis whose flaw is vanity - and argues with Aristotle that it is precisely their imperfect characters that make their concern with acting rightly possible.

chapters.file: ch24 - Elaine, Kramer, and Newman Not Wise.md
chapters.relation: Aeon Skoble argues Seinfeld explicates Aristotelian virtue ethics against utilitarian and Kantian rivals: Jerry's 'I don't want to be an orgy guy' and George's fear of becoming 'one of those guys' ask what sort of person to be, not which rule to follow. George's 'do the opposite' in 'The Opposite' is an update of the Delphic oracle - only he who recognizes his own idiocy (Socratic ignorance) can act well, with Jerry deducing the logic and serving as his phronemos, alongside Superman. Elaine's rule-worship and Jujyfruits utilitarianism backfire, Kramer lacks the social dialectic virtue needs, and the ironic appeals to Newman as arbiter expose the paradox that choosing a role model wisely already requires the wisdom one lacks.

Theodore Schick uses the Latham Good Samaritan law to argue that doing nothing can be something: against Jackie Chiles' bystander defense he sets the French bad-Samaritan statute, Thomson's Henry Fonda cases (distinguishing supererogatory aid from the duty of the 'minimally decent Samaritan'), and Rachels' Smith/Jones pair - Jones lets the child drown and is exactly as culpable as killer Smith - to show a duty of easy rescue exists, so the gang's failure to dial 911 on Jerry's cell phone deserved punishment. But in the 'Crime and Character' section he argues the trial itself was rigged: character evidence was inadmissible, and the four are not bad people, just people who failed their duty once.

holes.name: Instrumental Rationality (means-end reasoning)
holes.what: Reasoning that evaluates an action solely by whether it is a reliable and feasible means to the agent's desired ends, independent of whether those ends or the act are moral.
holes.why: Chapter 19's entire verdict on George's 'do the opposite' strategy is a decision-theoretic test of reliability and feasibility (minimal/medial/maximal rationality) that no existing slug covers.

holes.name: Slavoj Žižek
holes.what: Slovenian philosopher (b. 1949) fusing Marx, Hegel and Lacan; theorist of 'performative ideology' and cynical distance in The Sublime Object of Ideology.
holes.why: Chapter 20's framework is Žižek's account of ideology: we know the J. Peterman catalogue is fiction ('fetishists in practice, not in theory') yet it still regulates our buying.

holes.name: Jacques Lacan
holes.what: French psychoanalyst (1901-1981) of the Symbolic Order, the Imaginary, and the subject as lack ('reality is structured like a fiction').
holes.why: Chapter 20 grounds its claim that the self is an ideological fiction with nothing behind the mask in Lacan's Symbolic Order and the empty 'subject par excellence.'

holes.name: Philosophy of Humor (the comic)
holes.what: Theories of what makes things funny - incongruity, superiority, relief - and the contrast between comedy and tragedy as ways of seeing.
holes.why: Chapter 21 advances its own humor theory - we laugh at the significance of the insignificant and cry at the insignificance of the significant - and the taxonomy has no humor or aesthetics-of-the-comic concept.

holes.name: The Duty to Rescue (bad Samaritan laws)
holes.what: The claim that morality and law may require positive aid to those in peril (positive rights and easy rescues), not merely non-interference.
holes.why: Chapter 25's reading of the finale's Good Samaritan law turns on whether bystanders like the gang owe a duty of easy rescue, with supererogation vs the minimally decent Samaritan - no existing slug covers this.
